nodes.name: Euclidean space with norm and Lebesgue measure
nodes.statement: More precisely, let $\mathbb{R}^d$ be the Euclidean vector space equipped with distance $\|\cdot\|$ and Lebesgue measure $\mathrm{Vol}(\cdot)$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Open ball
nodes.statement: For $x\in\mathbb{R}^d$ and $r\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}$ we denote by $B_d(x,r)$ the open ball in $\mathbb{R}^d$ with center $x$ and radius $r$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Sphere packing
nodes.statement:
Let $X\subset \mathbb{R}^d$ be a discrete set of points such that $\|x-y\|\geq2$ for any distinct $x,y\in X$. Then the union
$$\mathcal{P}=\bigcup_{x\in X} B_d(x,1)$$ is a \emph{sphere packing}.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: A sphere packing is a union of unit balls centred at a discrete set of points at mutual distance at least 2.

nodes.name: Lattice sphere packing
nodes.statement: If $X$ is a lattice in $\mathbb{R}^d$ then we say that $\mathcal{P}$ is a \emph{lattice sphere packing}.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Finite density of a packing
nodes.statement:
The \emph{finite density} of a packing $\mathcal{P}$ is defined as
$$\Delta_{\mathcal{P}}(r):=\frac{\mathrm{Vol}(\mathcal{P}\cap B_d(0,r))}{\mathrm{Vol}(B_d(0,r))},\quad r>0.$$
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Density of a packing
nodes.statement:
We define the \emph{density} of a packing $\mathcal{P}$ as the limit superior
$$\Delta_{\mathcal{P}}:=\limsup\limits_{r\to\infty}\Delta_{\mathcal{P}}(r). $$
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Sphere packing constant
nodes.statement:
The number be want to know is the supremum over all possible packing densities
$$\Delta_d:=\sup\limits_{\substack{\mathcal{P}\subset\mathbb{R}^d\\ \scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{sphere}\;\mathrm{packing}}}\Delta_{\mathcal{P}}, $$
                         called the \emph{sphere packing constant}.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.genus: supremum over all possible packing densities

nodes.name: Density in dimension 1
nodes.statement: Trivially, in dimension~$1$ we have $\Delta_1=1$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Thue-Fejes Toth theorem (hexagonal packing is optimal in dimension 2)
nodes.statement: It has long been known  that a best packing in dimension $2$ is the familiar hexagonal lattice packing, in which each disk is touching six others.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
conclusions: a best packing in dimension $2$ is the familiar hexagonal lattice packing

nodes.name: Kepler conjecture
nodes.statement: Johannes Kepler conjectured in his essay ``On the six-cornered snowflake'' (1611) that no arrangement of equally sized spheres filling space has density greater than~$\frac{\pi}{\sqrt{18}}$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
conclusions: no arrangement of equally sized spheres filling space has density greater than~$\frac{\pi}{\sqrt{18}}$

nodes.name: Hales' theorem (Kepler conjecture)
nodes.statement: The Kepler conjecture was famously proven by T. Hales in 1998 \cite{Hales} and therefore we know that $\Delta_3=\frac{\pi}{\sqrt{18}}\approx0.74048$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: E8 lattice
nodes.statement:
Recall that the $E_8$-lattice $\Lambda_8\subset\mathbb{R}^8$ is given by
$$\Lambda_8=\{(x_i)\in\mathbb{Z}^8\cup(\mathbb{Z}+\textstyle\frac12\displaystyle )^8|\;\sum_{i=1}^8x_i\equiv 0\;(\mathrm{mod\;2})\}.$$
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Uniqueness of the E8 lattice
nodes.statement: $\Lambda_8$ is the unique up to isometry positive-definite, even, unimodular lattice of rank 8.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
conclusions: $\Lambda_8$ is the unique up to isometry positive-definite, even, unimodular lattice of rank 8

nodes.name: Minimal distance of the E8 lattice
nodes.statement: The minimal distance between two points in $\Lambda_8$ is $\sqrt{2}$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
conclusions: The minimal distance between two points in $\Lambda_8$ is $\sqrt{2}$

nodes.name: E8-lattice sphere packing
nodes.statement: The $E_8$-lattice sphere packing is the packing of unit balls with centers at $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\Lambda_8.$
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Sphere packing in dimension 8 (main theorem)
nodes.statement: No packing of unit balls in Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^8$ has density greater than that of the $E_8$-lattice packing.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
also_stated_at:
In this paper we prove that no packing of unit balls
in Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^8$ has density greater than that of the $E_8$-lattice packing.
The main result of this paper is the proof that $$\Delta_8=\frac{\pi^4}{384}\approx 0.25367.$$
conclusions: No packing of unit balls in Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^8$ has density greater than that of the $E_8$-lattice packing.
nodes.statement_short: The E8 lattice packing is the densest unit-ball packing in R^8.
nodes.label: thm: main

nodes.name: Uniqueness of the densest periodic packing in dimension 8
nodes.statement: Furthermore, our proof of Theorem~1 combined with arguments given in \cite[Section~8]{ElkiesCohn} implies that the $E_8$-lattice sphere packing is the unique periodic packing of maximal density.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
conclusions: the $E_8$-lattice sphere packing is the unique periodic packing of maximal density

nodes.statement: It is known \cite{BRV} that the linear programming bounds for the minimal number of points in an equal weight quadrature formula on the sphere $S^d$ are asymptotically optimal up to a constant depending on $d$.

nodes.name: Fourier transform
nodes.statement:
The \emph{Fourier transform} of an $L^1$~function $f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{C}$ is defined as
$$\mathcal{F}(f)(y)=\widehat{f}(y):=\int\limits_{\mathbb{R}^d} f(x)\,e^{-2\pi i x\cdot y}\,dx,\quad y\in\mathbb{R}^d $$
where $x\cdot y=\frac12\|x\|^2+\frac12\|y\|^2-\frac12\|x-y\|^2$ is the standard scalar product in $\mathbb{R}^d$.
nodes.section: 2 Linear programming bounds

nodes.name: Schwartz function
nodes.statement: A $C^\infty$~function $f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{C}$ is called a \emph{Schwartz function} if it tends to zero as $\|x\|\to\infty$ faster then any inverse power of $\|x\|$, and the same holds for all partial derivatives of $f$.

nodes.name: Admissible function
nodes.statement: We say that a function $f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{C}$ is \emph{admissible} if there is a constant $\delta>0$ such that $|f(x)|$ and $|\widehat{f}(x)|$ are bounded above by a constant times $(1+|x|)^{-d-\delta}$.

nodes.name: Cohn-Elkies linear programming bound
nodes.statement: (Cohn, Elkies \cite{ElkiesCohn}) Suppose that $f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}$ is an admissible function, is not identically zero, and satisfies: \begin{equation}f(x)\leq 0\mbox{ for } \|x\|\geq 1\end{equation} and \begin{equation}\widehat{f}(x)\geq0\mbox{ for all } x\in\mathbb{R}^d.\end{equation} Then the density of $d$-dimensional sphere packings is bounded above by $$\frac{f(0)}{\widehat{f}(0)}\cdot \frac{\pi^{\frac{d}{2}}}{2^d\,\Gamma(\textstyle \frac{d}{2}+1)}=\frac{f(0)}{\widehat{f}(0)}\cdot \mathrm{Vol}\,B_d(0,\frac 12).$$

conclusions:
the  density of  $d$-dimensional
 sphere packings is bounded above by

nodes.name: Poisson summation argument for the bound 2^4
nodes.statement:
The Poisson summation formula implies
 $$ \sum_{\ell\in\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\Lambda_8}f(\ell)= 2^4\,\sum_{\ell\in\sqrt{2}\Lambda_8}\widehat{f}(\ell).$$

nodes.name: Optimal function
nodes.statement: We say that an admissible function $f:\mathbb{R}^8\to\mathbb{R}$ is \emph{optimal} if it satisfies \eqref{eqn: Cohn-Elkies condition 1}, \eqref{eqn: Cohn-Elkies condition 2} and $f(0)/\widehat{f}(0)=2^4$.

nodes.statement: There exists a radial Schwartz function $g:\mathbb{R}^8\to\mathbb{R}$ which satisfies: \begin{align} g(x)&\leq 0\mbox{ for } \|x\|\geq \sqrt{2}, \\ \widehat{g}(x)&\geq0\mbox{ for all } x\in\mathbb{R}^8,\\ g(0)&=\widehat{g}(0)=1. \end{align} Moreover, the values $g(x)$ and $\widehat{g}(x)$ do not vanish for all vectors $x$ with $\|x\|^2\notin 2\mathbb{Z}_{>0}$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1
nodes.statement: Theorem \ref{thm: Cohn-Elkies} applied to the optimal function $f(x)=g(\sqrt{2}\,x)$ immediately implies Theorem \ref{thm: main}.

nodes.name: Upper half-plane
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbb{H}$ be the upper half-plane $\{z\in\mathbb{C}\mid\mathrm{Im}\,(z)>0\}$.
nodes.section: 3 Modular forms

nodes.name: Modular group and its action
nodes.statement:
The modular group $\Gamma(1):=\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$ acts on $\mathbb{H}$ by linear fractional transformations
$$\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{smallmatrix}\right)z:=\frac{az+b}{cz+d}.$$
nodes.section: 3 Modular forms

nodes.name: Principal congruence subgroup
nodes.statement:
Let $N$ be a positive integer. The \emph{level $N$ principal congruence subgroup} of $\Gamma(1)$ is
$$\Gamma(N):=\left\{\left.\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{smallmatrix}\right)\in\Gamma(1)\right|\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{smallmatrix}\right)\equiv\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\;\mathrm{mod}\;N\right\}.$$
nodes.section: 3 Modular forms

nodes.name: Congruence subgroup
nodes.statement: A subgroup $\Gamma\subset\Gamma(1)$ is called a \emph{congruence subgroup} if $\Gamma(N)\subset\Gamma$ for some $N\in\mathbb{N}$.
nodes.section: 3 Modular forms

nodes.name: Hecke congruence subgroup Gamma_0(N)
nodes.statement:
An important example of a congruence subgroup is
$$\Gamma_0(N):=\left\{\left.\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{smallmatrix}\right)\in\Gamma(1)\right|\;c\equiv0\;\mathrm{mod}\;N\right\}.$$
nodes.section: 3 Modular forms

nodes.name: Automorphy factor
nodes.statement:
Let $z\in\mathbb{H}$, $k\in\mathbb{Z}$, and $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{smallmatrix}\right)\in\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$. The \emph{automorphy factor} of weight $k$ is defined as
$$j_k(z,\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{smallmatrix}\right)):=(cz+d)^{-k}.$$
nodes.section: 3 Modular forms

nodes.name: Chain rule for the automorphy factor
nodes.statement:
The automorphy factor satisfies the \emph{chain rule}
$$j_k(z,\gamma_1\gamma_2)=j_k(z,\gamma_2)\,j_k(\gamma_2z,\gamma_1). $$
nodes.section: 3 Modular forms

nodes.name: Slash operator
nodes.statement:
Let $F$ be a  function on $\mathbb{H}$ and $\gamma\in\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$. Then the \emph{slash operator} acts on $F$ by
$$(F|_k\gamma)(z):=j_k(z,\gamma)\,F(\gamma z). $$
nodes.section: 3 Modular forms

nodes.name: Slash operator is a right action
nodes.statement:
The chain rule implies
$$F|_k\gamma_1\gamma_2=(F|_k\gamma_1)|_k\gamma_2.$$

nodes.statement: Let $M_k(\Gamma)$ be the space of modular forms of weight $k$ for the congruence subgroup $\Gamma$.

nodes.name: Finite dimensionality of M_k(Gamma)
nodes.statement: A key fact in the theory of modular forms is that the spaces $M_k(\Gamma)$ are finite dimensional.

nodes.name: Eisenstein series E_k
nodes.statement:
For an even integer $k\geq 4$ we define the \emph{weight $k$ Eisenstein series} as
\begin{equation} E_k(z):=\frac{1}{2\zeta(k)}\sum_{(c,d)\in\mathbb{Z}^2\backslash(0,0)}(cz+d)^{-k}.\end{equation}
nodes.section: 3 Modular forms

nodes.name: Modularity of E_k
nodes.statement: Since the sum converges absolutely, it is easy to see that $E_k\in M_k(\Gamma(1))$.
nodes.section: 3 Modular forms

nodes.name: Fourier expansion of Eisenstein series
nodes.statement:
The
Eisenstein series possesses the Fourier expansion
\begin{equation} E_k(z)=1+\frac{2}{\zeta(1-k)}\sum_{n=1}^\infty \sigma_{k-1}(n)\,e^{2\pi i n z}, \end{equation}
where $\sigma_{k-1}(n)\,=\,\sum_{d|n} d^{k-1}$.

nodes.label: prop: a(r) Fourier

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 1
nodes.statement: First, we prove that $a$ is a Schwartz function. From \eqref{eqn: j Fourier asymptotic}, \eqref{eqn: varphi Fourier asymptotic}, and \eqref{eqn: D varphi} we deduce that the Fourier coefficients of $\phi_0$ satisfy $$|c_{\phi_0}(n)|\leq2\,e^{4\pi\sqrt{n}}\quad n\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}.$$ Thus, there exists a positive constant $C$ such that $$|\phi_0(z)|\leq C\,e^{-2\pi \mathrm{Im}\,{z}}\qquad \mbox{for } \; \mathrm{Im}\,{z}>\frac 12.$$ We estimate the first summand in the right-hand side of \eqref{eqn: a(r) definition}. For $r\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ we have \begin{align*}&\Bigg|\int\limits_{-1}^{i}\phi_0\Big(\frac{-1}{z+1}\Big)\,(z+1)^2\,e^{\pi i r^2 z}\,dz\Bigg|=\Bigg|\int\limits_{i\infty}^{-1/(i+1)}\phi_0(z)\,z^{-4}\,e^{\pi i r^2 (-1/z-1)}\,dz\Bigg|\leq \\ &C_1\int\limits_{1/2}^{\infty}e^{-2\pi t}\,e^{-\pi r^2/t}\,dt\leq C_1\int\limits_{0}^{\infty}e^{-2\pi t}\,e^{-\pi r^2/t}\,dt=C_2\,r\,K_1(2\sqrt{2}\,\pi\,r) \end{align*} where $C_1$ and $C_2$ are some positive constants and $K_\alpha(x)$ is the modified Bessel function of the second kind defined as in \cite[Section~9.6]{Abramowitz}. This estimate also holds for the second and third summand in \eqref{eqn: a(r) definition}. For the last summand we have $$ \Bigg|\int\limits_{i}^{i\infty}\phi_0(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 z}\,dz\Bigg|\leq C\,\int\limits_{1}^{\infty} e^{-2\pi t}\,e^{-\pi r^2 t}\,dt=C_3\frac{e^{\pi(r^2+2)}}{r^2+2}.$$ Therefore, we arrive at $$|a(r)|\leq 4C_2\,r\,K_1(2\sqrt{2}\pi r)+2C_3\frac{e^{-\pi(r^2+2)}}{r^2+2}.$$ It is easy to see that the left hand side of this inequality decays faster then any inverse power of $r$. Analogous estimates can be obtained for all derivatives $\frac{d^k}{dr^k}a(r)$. Now we show that $a$ is an eigenfunction of the Fourier transform. We recall that the Fourier transform of a Gaussian function is \begin{equation}\mathcal{F}(e^{\pi i \|x\|^2 z})(y)=z^{-4}\,e^{\pi i \|y\|^2 \,(\frac{-1}{z}) }.\end{equation} Next, we exchange the contour integration with respect to $z$ variable and Fourier transform with respect to $x$ variable in \eqref{eqn: a(r) definition}. This can be done, since the corresponding double integral converges absolutely. In this way we obtain \begin{align*} \widehat{a}(y)=&\int\limits_{-1}^i\phi_0\Big(\frac{-1}{z+1}\Big)\,(z+1)^2\,z^{-4}\,e^{\pi i \|y\|^2 \,(\frac{-1}{z})}\,dz +\int\limits_{1}^i\phi_0\Big(\frac{-1}{z-1}\Big)\,(z-1)^2\,z^{-4}\,e^{\pi i \|y\|^2 \,(\frac{-1}{z})}\,dz\\ -&2\int\limits_{0}^i\phi_0\Big(\frac{-1}{z}\Big)\,z^2\,z^{-4}\,e^{\pi i \|y\|^2 \,(\frac{-1}{z})}\,dz +2\int\limits_{i}^{i\infty}\phi_0(z)\,z^{-4}\,e^{\pi i \|y\|^2 \,(\frac{-1}{z})}\,dz. \end{align*} Now we make a change of variables $w=\frac{-1}{z}$. We obtain \begin{align*} \widehat{a}(y)=&\int\limits_{1}^i\phi_0\Big(1-\frac{1}{w-1}\Big)\,(\frac{-1}{w}+1)^2\,w^{2}\,e^{\pi i \|y\|^2 \,w}\,dw\\ +&\int\limits_{-1}^i\phi_0\Big(1-\frac{1}{w+1}\Big)\,(\frac{-1}{w}-1)^2\,w^2\,e^{\pi i \|y\|^2 \,w}\,dw\\ -&2\int\limits_{i \infty}^i\phi_0(w)\,e^{\pi i \|y\|^2 \,w}\,dw +2\int\limits_{i}^{0}\phi_0\Big(\frac{-1}{w}\Big)\,w^{2}\,e^{\pi i \|y\|^2 \,w}\,dw. \end{align*} Since $\phi_0$ is $1$-periodic we have \begin{align*} \widehat{a}(y)\,=\,&\int\limits_{1}^i\phi_0\Big(\frac{-1}{z-1}\Big)\,(z-1)^2\,e^{\pi i \|y\|^2 \,z}\,dz +\int\limits_{-1}^i\phi_0\Big(\frac{-1}{z+1}\Big)\,(z+1)^2\,e^{\pi i \|y\|^2 \,z}\,dz\\ +&2\int\limits_{i}^{i\infty}\phi_0(z)\,e^{\pi i \|y\|^2 \,z}\,dz -2\int\limits_{0}^{i}\phi_0\Big(\frac{-1}{z}\Big)\,z^{2}\,e^{\pi i \|y\|^2 \,z}\,dz\\ \,=\,&a(y). \end{align*} This finishes the proof of the proposition.

nodes.name: Double-zero integral representation of a
nodes.statement: For $r>\sqrt{2}$ we can express $a(r)$ in the following form \begin{equation} a(r)=-4\sin(\pi r^2/2)^2\,\int\limits_{0}^{i\infty}\phi_0\Big(\frac{-1}{z}\Big)\,z^2\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz. \end{equation}

nodes.statement_short: For r>sqrt2, a(r) = -4 sin^2(pi r^2/2) times a single contour integral, exhibiting double zeroes.
nodes.label: prop: a(r) double zeroes

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2
nodes.statement: We denote the right hand side of \eqref{eqn: a double zeroes} by $d(r)$. It is easy to see that $d(r)$ is well-defined. Indeed, from the transformation formula \eqref{eqn: phi0 transform} and the expansions \eqref{eqn: phi fourier0}--\eqref{eqn: phi fourier4} we obtain \begin{align*} \phi_0\Big(\frac{-1}{it}\Big)=&O(e^{-2\pi/t})\quad\mbox{as}\;t\to 0\\ \phi_0\Big(\frac{-1}{it}\Big)=&O(t^{-2}\,e^{2\pi t})\quad\mbox{as}\;t\to \infty \end{align*} Hence, the integral \eqref{eqn: a double zeroes} converges absolutely for $r>\sqrt{2}$. We can write \begin{align*} d(r)=&\int\limits_{-1}^{i\infty-1}\phi_0\Big(\frac{-1}{z+1}\Big)\,(z+1)^2\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz- 2\int\limits_{0}^{i\infty}\phi_0\Big(\frac{-1}{z}\Big)\,z^2\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz\\ +&\int\limits_{1}^{i\infty+1}\phi_0\Big(\frac{-1}{z-1}\Big)\,(z-1)^2\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz. \end{align*} From \eqref{eqn: phi0 transform} we deduce that if $r>\sqrt{2}$ then $\phi_0\Big(\frac{-1}{z}\Big)\,z^2\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\to 0$ as $\mathrm{Im}\,(z)\to\infty$. Therefore, we can deform the paths of integration and rewrite \begin{align*} d(r)=&\int\limits_{-1}^{i}\phi_0\Big(\frac{-1}{z+1}\Big)\,(z+1)^2\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz +\int\limits_{i}^{i\infty}\phi_0\Big(\frac{-1}{z+1}\Big)\,(z+1)^2\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz\\ -2&\int\limits_{0}^{i}\phi_0\Big(\frac{-1}{z}\Big)\,z^2\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz -2\int\limits_{i}^{i\infty}\phi_0\Big(\frac{-1}{z}\Big)\,z^2\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz\\ +&\int\limits_{1}^{i}\phi_0\Big(\frac{-1}{z-1}\Big)\,(z-1)^2\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz +\int\limits_{i}^{i\infty}\phi_0\Big(\frac{-1}{z-1}\Big)\,(z-1)^2\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz. \end{align*} Now from \eqref{eqn: phi0 transform} we find \begin{align*}&\phi_0\Big(\frac{-1}{z+1}\Big)\,(z+1)^2-2\phi_0\Big(\frac{-1}{z}\Big)\,z^2+ \phi_0\Big(\frac{-1}{z-1}\Big)\,(z-1)^2=\\ &\phi_0(z+1)\,(z+1)^2-2\phi_0(z)\,z^2+\phi_0(z-1)\,(z-1)^2\\ &-\frac{12i}{\pi}\,\Big(\phi_{-2}(z+1)\,(z+1)-2\phi_{-2}(z)\,z+\phi_{-2}(z-1)\,(z-1)\Big)\\ &-\frac{36}{\pi^2}\Big(\phi_{-4}(z+1)-2\phi_{-4}(z)+\phi_{-4}(z-1)\Big)=\\ &2\phi_0(z). \end{align*} Thus, we obtain \begin{align*} d(r)=&\int\limits_{-1}^{i}\phi_0\Big(\frac{-1}{z+1}\Big)\,(z+1)^2\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz -2\int\limits_{0}^{i}\phi_0\Big(\frac{-1}{z}\Big)\,z^2\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz\\ +&\int\limits_{1}^{i}\phi_0\Big(\frac{-1}{z-1}\Big)\,(z-1)^2\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz +2\int\limits_{i}^{i\infty}\phi_0(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz=a(r). \end{align*} This finishes the proof.

nodes.name: Laplace-type integral representation of a
nodes.statement: For $r\geq0$ we have \begin{align}a(r)=&4i\,\sin(\pi r^2/2)^2\,\Bigg(\frac{36}{\pi^3\,(r^2-2)}-\frac{8640}{\pi^3\,r^4}+\frac{18144}{\pi^3\,r^2}\\ +&\int\limits_0^\infty\,\left(t^2\,\phi_0\Big(\frac{i}{t}\Big)-\frac{36}{\pi^2}\,e^{2\pi t}+\frac{8640}{\pi}\,t-\frac{18144}{\pi^2}\right)\,e^{-\pi r^2 t}\,dt \Bigg) .\notag\end{align} The integral converges absolutely for all $r\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$.
nodes.section: 4 Fourier eigenfunctions with double zeroes at lattice points
conclusions: The integral converges absolutely for all $r\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$.
nodes.statement_short: Integral formula for a(r), r>=0, subtracting the growing terms of t^2 phi_0(i/t).
nodes.label: prop: a another integral

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3
nodes.statement: Suppose that $r>\sqrt{2}$. Then by Proposition~\ref{prop: a(r) double zeroes} $$a(r)=4i\,\sin(\pi r^2/2)^2\,\int\limits_{0}^{\infty}\phi_0(i/t)\,t^2\,e^{-\pi r^2 t}\,dt. $$ From \eqref{eqn: phi fourier0}--\eqref{eqn: phi0 transform} we obtain \begin{equation} \phi_0(i/t)\,t^2=\frac{36}{\pi^2}\,e^{2 \pi t}-\frac{8640}{\pi}\,t+\frac{18144}{\pi^2}+O(t^2\,e^{-2\pi t})\quad\mbox{as}\;t\to\infty. \end{equation} For $r>\sqrt{2}$ we have \begin{equation} \int\limits_0^\infty \left(\frac{36}{\pi^2}\,e^{2 \pi t}+\frac{8640}{\pi}\,t+\frac{18144}{\pi^2}\right)\,e^{-\pi r^2 t}\,dt =\frac{36}{\pi^3\,(r^2-2)}-\frac{8640}{\pi^3\,r^4}+\frac{18144}{\pi^3\,r^2}.\end{equation} Therefore, the identity \eqref{eqn: a another integral} holds for $r>\sqrt{2}$. On the other hand, from the definition~\eqref{eqn: a(r) definition} we see that $a(r)$ is analytic in some neighborhood of $[0,\infty)$. The asymptotic expansion~\eqref{eqn: phi asymptotic} implies that the right hand side of \eqref{eqn: a another integral} is also analytic in some neighborhood of $[0,\infty)$. Hence, the identity \eqref{eqn: a another integral} holds on the whole interval $[0,\infty)$. This finishes the proof of the proposition.
nodes.section: 4 Fourier eigenfunctions with double zeroes at lattice points
nodes.statement_short: Valid for r>sqrt2 by Proposition 2 and the asymptotics of phi_0; extend to [0,infinity) by analytic continuation.

nodes.name: Proof that h lies in M^!_{-2}(Gamma_0(2))
nodes.statement:
Indeed, first we check that $h|_{-2}\gamma=h$
for all $\gamma\in\Gamma_0(2)$. Since the group $\Gamma_0(2)$ is generated by elements
$\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\2&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ and $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$
it suffices to check that $h$ is invariant under their action. This follows immediately
from \eqref{eqn: theta transform S}--\eqref{eqn: theta transform T} and \eqref{eqn: h define}. Next we analyze the poles of $h$.
It is known \cite[Chapter~I Lemma~4.1]{Mumford} that $\theta_{10}$ has no zeros in the upper-half plane and hence $h$ has poles only at the cusps.

nodes.statement_short: Check invariance on generators of Gamma_0(2) via theta transformation laws; theta_10 has no zeros so poles are at cusps.

nodes.name: b is a Schwartz Fourier eigenfunction with eigenvalue -1
nodes.statement: The function $b$ defined by \eqref{eqn: b(r) definition} belongs to the Schwartz space and satisfies $$\widehat{b}(x)=-b(x). $$
nodes.section: 4 Fourier eigenfunctions with double zeroes at lattice points
assumptions: The function $b$ defined by \eqref{eqn: b(r) definition}
nodes.label: prop: b(r) Fourier

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 5
nodes.statement: Here, we repeat the arguments used in the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop: a(r) Fourier}. First we show that $b$ is a Schwartz function. We have \begin{align*} &\int\limits_{-1}^{i}\psi_T(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 z}\,dz=\int\limits_{0}^{i+1}\psi_I(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 (z-1)}\,dz=\\ &\int\limits_{i\infty}^{-1/(i+1)}\psi_I\Big(\frac{-1}{z}\Big)\,e^{\pi i r^2 (-1/z-1)}\,z^{-2}\,dz=\int\limits_{i\infty}^{-1/(i+1)}\psi_S(z)\,z^{-4}\,e^{\pi i r^2 (-1/z-1)}\,dz.\\ \end{align*} There exists a positive constant $C$ such that $$|\psi_S(z)|\leq C\,e^{-\pi\,\mathrm{Im}\,{z}}\quad\mbox{for }\;\mathrm{Im}\,{z}>\frac12.$$ Thus, as in the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop: a(r) Fourier} we estimate the first summand in the left-hand side of~\eqref{eqn: b(r) definition} $$\Bigg|\int\limits_{-1}^i \psi_T(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 z}\,dz \Bigg|\leq C_1\,r\,K_1(2\pi r).$$ We combine this inequality with analogous estimates for the other three summands and obtain $$|b(r)|\leq C_2\,r\,K_1(2\pi r)+C_3\,\frac{e^{-\pi(r^2+1)}}{r^2+1}.$$ Here $C_1$, $C_2$, and $C_3$ are some positive constants. Similar estimates hold for all derivatives $\frac{d^k}{d^k r} b(r)$. Now we prove that $b$ is an eigenfunction of the Fourier transform. We use identity~\eqref{eqn: Gaussian Fourier} and interchange contour integration in $z$ and Fourier transform in $x$. Thus we obtain \begin{align*} \mathcal{F}(b)(x)= & \int\limits_{-1}^{i}\psi_T(z)\,z^{-4}\,e^{\pi i \|x\|^2 (\frac{-1}{z})}\,dz + \int\limits_{1}^{i}\psi_T(z)\,z^{-4}\,e^{\pi i \|x\|^2 (\frac{-1}{z})}\,dz \\ -& 2\,\int\limits_{0}^{i}\psi_I(z)\,z^{-4}\,e^{\pi i \|x\|^2 (\frac{-1}{z})}\,dz - 2\,\int\limits_{i}^{i\infty}\psi_S(z)\,z^{-4}\,e^{\pi i \|x\|^2 (\frac{-1}{z})}\,dz. \end{align*} We make the change of variables $w=\frac{-1}{z}$ and arrive at \begin{align*} \mathcal{F}(b)(x)= & \int\limits_{1}^{i}\psi_T\Big(\frac{-1}{w}\Big)\,w^{2}\,e^{\pi i \|x\|^2 w}\,dw + \int\limits_{-1}^{i}\psi_T\Big(\frac{-1}{w}\Big)\,w^{2}\,e^{\pi i \|x\|^2 w}\,dw \\ -& 2\,\int\limits_{i\infty}^{i}\psi_I\Big(\frac{-1}{w}\Big)\,w^{2}\,e^{\pi i \|x\|^2 w}\,dw - 2\,\int\limits_{i}^{0}\psi_S\Big(\frac{-1}{w}\Big)\,w^{2}\,e^{\pi i \|x\|^2 w}\,dw. \end{align*} Now we observe that the definitions \eqref{eqn: psi I define}--\eqref{eqn: psi S define} imply \begin{align*}\psi_T|_{-2}S=&-\psi_T ,\\ \psi_I|_{-2}S=&\psi_S ,\\ \psi_S|_{-2}S=&\psi_I. \\ \end{align*} Therefore, we arrive at \begin{align*} \mathcal{F}(b)(x)= & \int\limits_{1}^{i}-\psi_T(z)\,e^{\pi i \|x\|^2 z}\,dz + \int\limits_{-1}^{i}-\psi_T(z)\,e^{\pi i \|x\|^2 z}\,dz \\ +& 2\,\int\limits_{i}^{i\infty}\psi_S(z)\,e^{\pi i \|x\|^2 z}\,dz + 2\,\int\limits_{0}^{i}\psi_I(z)\,e^{\pi i \|x\|^2 w}\,dw. \end{align*} Now from~\eqref{eqn: b(r) definition} we see that $$ \mathcal{F}(b)(x)=-b(x). $$

nodes.statement_short: Same scheme as Proposition 1: decay of psi_S gives Schwartz bounds; Fourier-transform the Gaussian and use the S-action on psi's.

nodes.name: Double-zero integral representation of b
nodes.statement: For $r>\sqrt{2}$ function $b(r)$ can be expressed as \begin{equation} b(r)=-4\sin(\pi r^2/2)^2\,\int\limits_{0}^{i\infty}\psi_I(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 4 Fourier eigenfunctions with double zeroes at lattice points
nodes.label: prop: b(r) double zeroes

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 6
nodes.statement: We denote the right hand side of~\eqref{eqn: b double zeroes} by $c(r)$. First, we check that $c(r)$ is well-defined. We have \begin{align*} \psi_I(it)=O(t^{2}\,e^{-\pi/t})\quad\mbox{as}\;t\to 0,\\ \psi_I(it)=O(e^{2\pi t})\quad\mbox{as}\;t\to\infty. \end{align*} Therefore, the integral~\eqref{eqn: b double zeroes} converges for $r>\sqrt{2}$. Then we rewrite it in the following way: $$c(r)=\int\limits_{-1}^{i\infty-1}\psi_I(z+1)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz-2\int\limits_{0}^{i\infty}\psi_I(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz+ \int\limits_{1}^{i\infty+1}\psi_I(z-1)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz.$$ From the Fourier expansion~\eqref{eqn: psi fourier I} we know that $\psi_I(z)=e^{-2\pi i z}+O(1)$ as $\mathrm{Im}\,(z)\to\infty$. By assumption $r^2>2$, hence we can deform the path of integration and write \begin{align} \int\limits_{-1}^{i\infty-1}\psi_I(z+1)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz=& \int\limits_{-1}^{i}\psi_T(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz+\int\limits_{i}^{i\infty}\psi_T(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz,\\ \int\limits_{1}^{i\infty+1}\psi_I(z-1)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz=& \int\limits_{-1}^{i}\psi_T(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz+\int\limits_{i}^{i\infty}\psi_T(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz. \end{align} We have \begin{align}c(r)=&\int\limits_{-1}^{i}\psi_T(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz+\int\limits_{1}^{i}\psi_T(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz -2\int\limits_{0}^{i}\psi_I(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz\\ &+2\int\limits_{i}^{i\infty}(\psi_T(z)-\psi_I(z))\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz.\nonumber \end{align} Next, we check that the functions $\psi_I,\psi_T$, and $\psi_S$ satisfy the following identity: \begin{equation}\psi_T+\psi_S=\psi_I.\end{equation} Indeed, from definitions \eqref{eqn: psi I define}-\eqref{eqn: psi S define} we get \begin{align*}\psi_T+\psi_S=&(h-h|_{-2}ST)|_{-2}T+(h-h|_{-2}ST)|_{-2}S\\ =&h|_{-2}T-h|_{-2}ST^2+h|_{-2}S-h|_{-2}STS.\end{align*} Note that $ST^2S$ belongs to $\Gamma_0(2)$. Thus, since $h\in M^!_{-2}\Gamma_0(2)$ we get $$\psi_T+\psi_S=h|_{-2}T-h|_{-2}STS. $$ Now we observe that $T$ and $STS(ST)^{-1}$ are also in $\Gamma_0(2)$. Therefore, $$\psi_T+\psi_S=h|_{-2}T-h|_{-2}STS=h-h|_{-2}ST=\psi_I.$$ Combining \eqref{eqn: c1} and \eqref{eqn: c2} we find \begin{align*}c(r)=&\int\limits_{-1}^{i}\psi_T(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz+\int\limits_{1}^{i}\psi_T(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz -2\int\limits_{0}^{i}\psi_I(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz\\ &-2\int\limits_{i}^{i\infty}\psi_S(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz\\ =&b(r). \end{align*}

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 7
nodes.statement: The proof is analogous to the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop: a another integral}. First, suppose that $r>\sqrt{2}$. Then by Proposition~\ref{prop: b(r) double zeroes} $$b(r)=4i\,\sin(\pi r^2/2)^2\,\int\limits_{0}^{\infty}\psi_I(it)\,e^{-\pi r^2 t}\,dt. $$ From \eqref{eqn: psi fourier I} we obtain \begin{equation} \psi_I(it)=e^{2\pi t}+144+O(e^{-\pi t})\quad\mbox{as}\;t\to\infty. \end{equation} For $r>\sqrt{2}$ we have \begin{equation} \int\limits_0^\infty \left(e^{2\pi t}+144\right)\,e^{-\pi r^2 t}\,dt =\frac{1}{\pi\,(r^2-2)}+\frac{144}{\pi\,r^2}.\end{equation} Therefore, the identity \eqref{eqn: a another integral} holds for $r>\sqrt{2}$. On the other hand, from the definition \eqref{eqn: b(r) definition} we see that $b(r)$ is analytic in some neighborhood of $[0,\infty)$. The asymptotic expansion \eqref{eqn: psi asymptotic} implies that the right hand side of \eqref{eqn: b another integral} is also analytic in some neighborhood of $[0,\infty)$. Hence, the identity \eqref{eqn: b another integral} holds on the whole interval $[0,\infty)$. This finishes the proof of the proposition.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorems 3 and 2
nodes.statement: First, we prove that \eqref{eqn: g1} holds. By Propositions~\ref{prop: a(r) double zeroes} and \ref{prop: b(r) double zeroes} we know that for $r>\sqrt{2}$ \begin{equation} g(r)=\frac{\pi}{2160}\,\sin(\pi r^2/2)^2\,\int\limits_0^\infty A(t)\,e^{-\pi r^2 t}\,dt\end{equation} where $$A(t)=-t^2\phi_0(i/t)-\frac{36}{\pi^2}\,\psi_I(it).$$ Our goal is to show that $A(t)<0\quad\mbox{for}\;t\in(0,\infty).$ The function $A(t)$ is plotted in Figure~\ref{fig: A}. \begin{figure}[h!] \caption{Plot of the functions $A(t)$, $A^{(2)}_0(t)=-\frac{368640}{\pi^2}\,t^2\,e^{-\pi /t}$, and $A^{(1)}_\infty(t)=-\frac{72}{\pi^2}\,e^{2\pi t}+\frac{8640}{\pi}t-\frac{23328}{\pi^2}$.} \centering \includegraphics[width=300 pt]{e8plot_A.pdf} \end{figure} \noindent We observe that we can compute the values of $A(t)$ for $t\in(0,\infty)$ with any given precision. Indeed, from identities \eqref{eqn: phi0 transform} and \eqref{eqn: psi S define} we obtain the following two presentations for $A(t)$ \begin{align*} A(t)=&-t^2\phi_0(i/t)+\frac{36}{\pi^2}\,t^2\,\psi_S(i/t),\\ A(t)=&-t^2\phi_0(it)+\frac{12}{\pi}\,t\,\phi_{-2}(it)-\frac{36}{\pi^2}\,\phi_{-4}(it)-\frac{36}{\pi^2}\,\psi_I(it). \end{align*} For an integer $n\geq0$ let $A_0^{(n)}$ and $A_{\infty}^{(n)}$ be the functions such that \begin{align} A(t)=&A_0^{(n)}(t)+O(t^2\,e^{-\pi n /t})\quad\mbox{as}\;t\to0,\\ A(t)=&A_\infty^{(n)}(t)+O(t^2\,e^{-\pi n t})\quad\mbox{as}\;t\to\infty. \end{align} For each $n\geq 0$ we can compute these functions from the Fourier expansions \eqref{eqn: phi fourier0}--\eqref{eqn: phi fourier4}, \eqref{eqn: psi fourier I}, and \eqref{eqn: psi fourier S}. For example, from \eqref{eqn: phi fourier4}--\eqref{eqn: phi fourier0} and \eqref{eqn: psi fourier I} we compute \begin{align*}A_\infty^{(6)}(t)=&\scriptstyle-\tfrac{72}{\pi ^2}\, e^{2 \pi t}-\tfrac{23328}{\pi ^2}+\tfrac{184320}{\pi ^2}\, e^{-\pi t}-\tfrac{5194368}{\pi ^2}\, e^{-2 \pi t}+\tfrac{22560768}{\pi ^2}\, e^{-3 \pi t}-\tfrac{250583040}{\pi ^2}\, e^{-4 \pi t}+\tfrac{869916672 }{\pi ^2}\,e^{-5 \pi t}\\&\scriptstyle+t(\tfrac{8640}{\pi }+\tfrac{2436480}{\pi }\, e^{-2 \pi t}+\tfrac{113011200 }{\pi }\,e^{-4 \pi t})-t^2(518400\,e^{-2 \pi t}+31104000\,e^{-4 \pi t}). \end{align*} From \eqref{eqn: phi fourier4}--\eqref{eqn: phi fourier0} and \eqref{eqn: psi fourier S} we compute $$A_0^{(6)}(t)=t^2(-\tfrac{368640}{\pi ^2}\, e^{-\pi/t}-518400\, e^{-2\pi/t}-\tfrac{45121536}{\pi ^2}\, e^{-3\pi/t}-31104000\,e^{-4\pi/t}-\tfrac{1739833344}{\pi ^2}\, e^{-5\pi/t}).$$ Moreover, from the convergent asymptotic expansion for the Fourier coefficients of a weakly holomorphic modular form \cite[Proposition 1.12]{Bruinier} we find that the $n$-th Fourier coefficient $c_{\psi_I}(n)$ of $\psi_I$ satisfies \begin{equation}|c_{\psi_I}(n)|\leq e^{4\pi\sqrt{n}}\qquad n\in\tfrac 12 \mathbb{Z}_{>0}.\end{equation} Similar inequalities hold for the Fourier coefficients of $\psi_S$, $\phi_0$, $\phi_{-2}$, and $\phi_{-4}$: \begin{align} &|c_{\psi_S}(n)|\leq 2e^{4\pi\sqrt{n}}\qquad n\in\tfrac 12 \mathbb{Z}_{>0} ,\\ &|c_{\phi_0}(n)|\leq 2e^{4\pi\sqrt{n}}\qquad n\in \mathbb{Z}_{>0} ,\\ &|c_{\phi_{-2}}(n)|\leq e^{4\pi\sqrt{n}}\qquad n\in \mathbb{Z}_{>0},\\ &|c_{\phi_{-4}}(n)|\leq e^{4\pi\sqrt{n}}\qquad n\in \mathbb{Z}_{>0}. \end{align} Therefore, we can estimate the error terms in the asymptotic expansions \eqref{eqn: A asymptotic expansion 0} and \eqref{eqn: A asymptotic expansion infty} of $A(t)$ \begin{align*} \left|A(t)-A_0^{(m)}(t)\right|\leq& (t^2+\frac{36}{\pi^2})\,\sum_{n=m}^\infty 2e^{2\sqrt{2}\pi\sqrt{n}}\,e^{-\pi n/t},\\ \left|A(t)-A_\infty^{(m)}(t)\right|\leq& (t^2+\frac{12}{\pi}\,t+\frac{36}{\pi^2})\,\sum_{n=m}^\infty 2e^{2\sqrt{2}\pi\sqrt{n}}\,e^{-\pi nt}. \end{align*} For an integer $m\geq0$ we set \begin{align*} R^{(m)}_0:=&(t^2+\frac{36}{\pi^2})\,\sum_{n=m}^\infty 2e^{2\sqrt{2}\pi\sqrt{n}}\,e^{-\pi n/t},\\ R^{(m)}_\infty:=&(t^2+\frac{12}{\pi}\,t+\frac{36}{\pi^2})\,\sum_{n=m}^\infty 2e^{2\sqrt{2}\pi\sqrt{n}}\,e^{-\pi nt}. \end{align*} Using interval arithmetic we check that \begin{align*} &\left|R_0^{(6)}(t)\right|\leq\left|A_0^{(6)}(t)\right|\quad\mbox{ for }\;t\in(0,1],\\ &\left|R_\infty^{(6)}(t)\right|\leq\left|A_\infty^{(6)}(t)\right|\quad\mbox{ for }\;t\in[1,\infty),\\ &A_0^{(6)}(t)<0\quad\mbox{ for }\;t\in(0,1],\\ &A_\infty^{(6)}(t)<0\quad\mbox{ for }\;t\in[1,\infty). \end{align*} Thus, we see that $A(t)<0$ for $t\in (0,\infty)$. Then identity \eqref{eqn: g A} implies \eqref{eqn: g1}. Next, we prove \eqref{eqn: g2}. By Propositions~\ref{prop: a another integral} and~\ref{prop: b another integral} we know that for $r>0$ \begin{equation} \widehat{g}(r)=\frac{\pi}{2160}\,\sin(\pi r^2/2)^2\,\int\limits_0^\infty B(t)\,e^{-\pi r^2 t}\,dt\end{equation} where $$B(t)=-t^2\phi_0(i/t)+\frac{36}{\pi^2}\,\psi_I(it).$$ This function can also be written as \begin{align*} B(t)=&-t^2\phi_0(i/t)-\frac{36}{\pi^2}\,t^2\,\psi_S(i/t),\\ B(t)=&-t^2\phi_0(it)+\frac{12}{\pi}\,t\,\phi_{-2}(it)-\frac{36}{\pi^2}\,\phi_{-4}(it)+\frac{36}{\pi^2}\,\psi_I(it). \end{align*} Our aim is to prove that $B(t)>0$ for $t\in(0,\infty)$. A plot of $B(t)$ is given in Figure~\ref{fig:B}. \begin{figure}[h!] \caption{Plot of the functions $B(t)$, $B^{(2)}_0(t)=\frac{368640}{\pi^2}\,t^2\,e^{-\pi /t}$, and $B^{(1)}_\infty(t)=\frac{8640}{\pi}t-\frac{23328}{\pi^2}$.} \centering \includegraphics[width=300 pt]{e8plot_B.pdf} \end{figure} \noindent For $n\geq 0$ let $B_0^{(n)}$ and $B_{\infty}^{(n)}$ be the functions such that \begin{align*} B(t)=&B_0^{(n)}(t)+O(t^2\,e^{-\pi n /t})\quad\mbox{as}\;t\to0,\\ B(t)=&B_\infty^{(n)}(t)+O(t^2\,e^{-\pi n t})\quad\mbox{as}\;t\to\infty. \end{align*} We find \begin{align*}B_\infty^{(6)}(t)=&-\tfrac{12960}{\pi ^2}-\tfrac{184320}{\pi ^2}\,\scriptstyle e^{-\pi t}\displaystyle-\tfrac{116640}{\pi ^2} \,\scriptstyle e^{-2\pi t}\displaystyle-\tfrac{22560768}{\pi ^2}\,\scriptstyle e^{-3\pi t}\displaystyle+\tfrac{56540160}{\pi ^2}\,\scriptstyle e^{-4\pi t}\displaystyle-\tfrac{869916672 }{\pi ^2} \,\scriptstyle e^{-5\pi t}\displaystyle\\&+t(\tfrac{8640 }{\pi }+\tfrac{2436480}{\pi }\,\scriptstyle e^{-2\pi t}\displaystyle+\tfrac{113011200 }{\pi }\,\scriptstyle e^{-4\pi t}\textstyle)-t^2(\scriptstyle518400\,\scriptstyle e^{-2\pi t}\displaystyle+\scriptstyle31104000\,\scriptstyle e^{-4\pi t}\displaystyle) \end{align*} and $$B_0^{(6)}(t)= t^2(\tfrac{368640}{\pi ^2}\, e^{-\pi/t}-518400\, e^{-2 \pi /t}+\tfrac{45121536 }{\pi ^2}\,e^{-3 \pi/t}-31104000\, e^{-4 \pi/t}+\tfrac{1739833344 }{\pi ^2}\,e^{-5 \pi/t}) .$$ The estimates \eqref{eqn: Fourier estimate 1}--\eqref{eqn: Fourier estimate 5} imply that $$\left|B(t)-B_0^{(6)}(t)\right|\leq R_0^{(6)}(t)\quad\mbox{for}\;t\in(0,1]$$ and $$\left|B(t)-B_\infty^{(6)}(t)\right|\leq R_\infty^{(6)}(t)\quad\mbox{for}\;t\in[1,\infty).$$ Using interval arithmetic we verify that \begin{align*} &\left|R_0^{(6)}(t)\right|\leq\left|B_0^{(6)}(t)\right|\quad\mbox{ for }\;t\in(0,1],\\ &\left|R_\infty^{(6)}(t)\right|\leq\left|B_\infty^{(6)}(t)\right|\quad\mbox{ for }\;t\in[1,\infty),\\ &B_0^{(6)}(t)>0\quad\mbox{ for }\;t\in(0,1],\\ &B_\infty^{(6)}(t)>0\quad\mbox{ for }\;t\in[1,\infty). \end{align*} Now identity \eqref{eqn: g B} implies \eqref{eqn: g2}. Finally, the property \eqref{eqn: g3} readily follows from Proposition~\ref{prop: a values} and Proposition~\ref{prop: b values}. This finishes the proof of Theorems~\ref{thm: g1} and~\ref{thm: g}.

nodes.name: a is a Schwartz function
nodes.statement:
First, we prove that $a$ is a Schwartz function. From \eqref{eqn: j Fourier asymptotic}, \eqref{eqn: varphi Fourier asymptotic}, and \eqref{eqn: D varphi} we deduce that the Fourier coefficients of $\phi_0$ satisfy
$$|c_{\phi_0}(n)|\leq2\,e^{4\pi\sqrt{n}}\quad n\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}.$$ Thus, there exists a positive constant $C$ such that
$$|\phi_0(z)|\leq C\,e^{-2\pi \mathrm{Im}\,{z}}\qquad \mbox{for } \; \mathrm{Im}\,{z}>\frac 12.$$ We estimate the first summand in the right-hand side of \eqref{eqn: a(r) definition}.  For $r\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ we have
\begin{align*}&\Bigg|\int\limits_{-1}^{i}\phi_0\Big(\frac{-1}{z+1}\Big)\,(z+1)^2\,e^{\pi i r^2 z}\,dz\Bigg|=\Bigg|\int\limits_{i\infty}^{-1/(i+1)}\phi_0(z)\,z^{-4}\,e^{\pi i r^2 (-1/z-1)}\,dz\Bigg|\leq \\
 &C_1\int\limits_{1/2}^{\infty}e^{-2\pi t}\,e^{-\pi  r^2/t}\,dt\leq C_1\int\limits_{0}^{\infty}e^{-2\pi t}\,e^{-\pi  r^2/t}\,dt=C_2\,r\,K_1(2\sqrt{2}\,\pi\,r)
\end{align*}
where $C_1$ and $C_2$ are some positive constants and $K_\alpha(x)$ is the modified Bessel function of the second kind defined as in \cite[Section~9.6]{Abramowitz}. This estimate also holds for the second and third summand in \eqref{eqn: a(r) definition}.
For the last summand we have
$$ \Bigg|\int\limits_{i}^{i\infty}\phi_0(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 z}\,dz\Bigg|\leq C\,\int\limits_{1}^{\infty} e^{-2\pi t}\,e^{-\pi r^2 t}\,dt=C_3\frac{e^{\pi(r^2+2)}}{r^2+2}.$$
Therefore, we arrive at
$$|a(r)|\leq 4C_2\,r\,K_1(2\sqrt{2}\pi r)+2C_3\frac{e^{-\pi(r^2+2)}}{r^2+2}.$$
It is easy to see that the left hand side of this inequality decays faster then any inverse power of $r$. Analogous estimates can be obtained for all derivatives $\frac{d^k}{dr^k}a(r)$.

\begin{align*}
  \mathcal{F}(b)(x)= & \int\limits_{-1}^{i}\psi_T(z)\,z^{-4}\,e^{\pi i \|x\|^2 (\frac{-1}{z})}\,dz
    + \int\limits_{1}^{i}\psi_T(z)\,z^{-4}\,e^{\pi i \|x\|^2 (\frac{-1}{z})}\,dz \\
  -& 2\,\int\limits_{0}^{i}\psi_I(z)\,z^{-4}\,e^{\pi i \|x\|^2 (\frac{-1}{z})}\,dz
  - 2\,\int\limits_{i}^{i\infty}\psi_S(z)\,z^{-4}\,e^{\pi i \|x\|^2 (\frac{-1}{z})}\,dz.
\end{align*}
We make the change of variables $w=\frac{-1}{z}$ and arrive at
\begin{align*}
  \mathcal{F}(b)(x)= & \int\limits_{1}^{i}\psi_T\Big(\frac{-1}{w}\Big)\,w^{2}\,e^{\pi i \|x\|^2 w}\,dw
    + \int\limits_{-1}^{i}\psi_T\Big(\frac{-1}{w}\Big)\,w^{2}\,e^{\pi i \|x\|^2 w}\,dw \\
  -& 2\,\int\limits_{i\infty}^{i}\psi_I\Big(\frac{-1}{w}\Big)\,w^{2}\,e^{\pi i \|x\|^2 w}\,dw
  - 2\,\int\limits_{i}^{0}\psi_S\Big(\frac{-1}{w}\Big)\,w^{2}\,e^{\pi i \|x\|^2 w}\,dw.
\end{align*}
Now we observe that the definitions \eqref{eqn: psi I define}--\eqref{eqn: psi S define}   imply
\begin{align*}\psi_T|_{-2}S=&-\psi_T ,\\
\psi_I|_{-2}S=&\psi_S ,\\
\psi_S|_{-2}S=&\psi_I. \\
\end{align*}

\begin{align*}
  \mathcal{F}(b)(x)= & \int\limits_{1}^{i}-\psi_T(z)\,e^{\pi i \|x\|^2 z}\,dz
    + \int\limits_{-1}^{i}-\psi_T(z)\,e^{\pi i \|x\|^2 z}\,dz \\
  +& 2\,\int\limits_{i}^{i\infty}\psi_S(z)\,e^{\pi i \|x\|^2 z}\,dz
  + 2\,\int\limits_{0}^{i}\psi_I(z)\,e^{\pi i \|x\|^2 w}\,dw.
\end{align*}
Now from~\eqref{eqn: b(r) definition} we see that
$$ \mathcal{F}(b)(x)=-b(x). $$

nodes.name: S-action on psi's
nodes.statement:
Now we observe that the definitions \eqref{eqn: psi I define}--\eqref{eqn: psi S define}   imply
\begin{align*}\psi_T|_{-2}S=&-\psi_T ,\\
\psi_I|_{-2}S=&\psi_S ,\\
\psi_S|_{-2}S=&\psi_I. \\
\end{align*}
nodes.section: 4 Fourier eigenfunctions with double zeroes at lattice points
nodes.statement_short: S acts as psi_T -> -psi_T, psi_I <-> psi_S.

nodes.name: Rewrite transform
nodes.statement:
Therefore, we arrive at
\begin{align*}
  \mathcal{F}(b)(x)= & \int\limits_{1}^{i}-\psi_T(z)\,e^{\pi i \|x\|^2 z}\,dz
    + \int\limits_{-1}^{i}-\psi_T(z)\,e^{\pi i \|x\|^2 z}\,dz \\
  +& 2\,\int\limits_{i}^{i\infty}\psi_S(z)\,e^{\pi i \|x\|^2 z}\,dz
  + 2\,\int\limits_{0}^{i}\psi_I(z)\,e^{\pi i \|x\|^2 w}\,dw.
\end{align*}
nodes.section: 4 Fourier eigenfunctions with double zeroes at lattice points
nodes.statement_short: Substitute the S-action.

nodes.name: Conclude F(b)=-b
nodes.statement:
Now from~\eqref{eqn: b(r) definition} we see that
$$ \mathcal{F}(b)(x)=-b(x). $$
nodes.section: 4 Fourier eigenfunctions with double zeroes at lattice points
nodes.statement_short: Compare with the definition of b.

nodes.name: c(r) is well defined
nodes.section: 4 Fourier eigenfunctions with double zeroes at lattice points
nodes.statement_short: Name the right-hand side c(r) and check convergence.

nodes.name: Asymptotics of psi_I(it)
nodes.section: 4 Fourier eigenfunctions with double zeroes at lattice points
nodes.statement_short: Growth of psi_I(it) at 0 and infinity.

nodes.name: Convergence
nodes.statement: Therefore, the integral~\eqref{eqn: b double zeroes} converges for $r>\sqrt{2}$.
nodes.section: 4 Fourier eigenfunctions with double zeroes at lattice points
nodes.statement_short: Integral converges for r>sqrt2.

nodes.name: Rewrite c(r)
nodes.statement:
Then we rewrite it in the following way:
$$c(r)=\int\limits_{-1}^{i\infty-1}\psi_I(z+1)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz-2\int\limits_{0}^{i\infty}\psi_I(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz+
\int\limits_{1}^{i\infty+1}\psi_I(z-1)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz.$$
nodes.section: 4 Fourier eigenfunctions with double zeroes at lattice points
nodes.statement_short: Split into shifted integrals.

nodes.name: Leading term of psi_I
nodes.statement: From the Fourier expansion~\eqref{eqn: psi fourier I} we know that $\psi_I(z)=e^{-2\pi i z}+O(1)$ as $\mathrm{Im}\,(z)\to\infty$.
nodes.section: 4 Fourier eigenfunctions with double zeroes at lattice points
nodes.statement_short: psi_I = e^{-2 pi i z}+O(1) at i infinity.

nodes.name: Deform contours
nodes.statement:
By assumption $r^2>2$, hence we can deform the path of integration and write
\begin{align} \int\limits_{-1}^{i\infty-1}\psi_I(z+1)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz=&
\int\limits_{-1}^{i}\psi_T(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz+\int\limits_{i}^{i\infty}\psi_T(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz,\\
\int\limits_{1}^{i\infty+1}\psi_I(z-1)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz=&
\int\limits_{-1}^{i}\psi_T(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz+\int\limits_{i}^{i\infty}\psi_T(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz.
\end{align}
nodes.section: 4 Fourier eigenfunctions with double zeroes at lattice points
nodes.statement_short: Deform the shifted paths through i.

nodes.name: Combined expression for c(r)
nodes.statement:
We have
\begin{align} c(r)=&\int\limits_{-1}^{i}\psi_T(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz+\int\limits_{1}^{i}\psi_T(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz
-2\int\limits_{0}^{i}\psi_I(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz\\
&+2\int\limits_{i}^{i\infty}(\psi_T(z)-\psi_I(z))\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz.\nonumber
 \end{align}
nodes.section: 4 Fourier eigenfunctions with double zeroes at lattice points
nodes.statement_short: Collect terms into (c1).

nodes.name: Identity psi_T+psi_S=psi_I
nodes.statement:
Next, we check that the functions $\psi_I,\psi_T$, and $\psi_S$ satisfy the following identity:
\begin{equation} \psi_T+\psi_S=\psi_I.\end{equation}
Indeed, from definitions \eqref{eqn: psi I define}-\eqref{eqn: psi S define} we get
\begin{align*}\psi_T+\psi_S=&(h-h|_{-2}ST)|_{-2}T+(h-h|_{-2}ST)|_{-2}S\\
=&h|_{-2}T-h|_{-2}ST^2+h|_{-2}S-h|_{-2}STS.\end{align*}
Note that $ST^2S$ belongs to $\Gamma_0(2)$. Thus, since $h\in M^!_{-2}\Gamma_0(2)$ we get
$$\psi_T+\psi_S=h|_{-2}T-h|_{-2}STS. $$
Now we observe that $T$ and $STS(ST)^{-1}$ are also in $\Gamma_0(2)$. Therefore,
$$\psi_T+\psi_S=h|_{-2}T-h|_{-2}STS=h-h|_{-2}ST=\psi_I.$$
nodes.section: 4 Fourier eigenfunctions with double zeroes at lattice points
nodes.statement_short: Prove psi_T+psi_S=psi_I.

nodes.name: Expand definitions
nodes.section: 4 Fourier eigenfunctions with double zeroes at lattice points
nodes.statement_short: Expand via slash operators.

nodes.name: Use ST^2S in Gamma_0(2)
nodes.statement:
Note that $ST^2S$ belongs to $\Gamma_0(2)$. Thus, since $h\in M^!_{-2}\Gamma_0(2)$ we get
$$\psi_T+\psi_S=h|_{-2}T-h|_{-2}STS. $$
nodes.section: 4 Fourier eigenfunctions with double zeroes at lattice points
nodes.statement_short: Invariance of h cancels two terms.

nodes.name: Use T, STS(ST)^{-1} in Gamma_0(2)
nodes.statement:
Now we observe that $T$ and $STS(ST)^{-1}$ are also in $\Gamma_0(2)$. Therefore,
$$\psi_T+\psi_S=h|_{-2}T-h|_{-2}STS=h-h|_{-2}ST=\psi_I.$$
nodes.section: 4 Fourier eigenfunctions with double zeroes at lattice points
nodes.statement_short: Further invariance gives psi_I.

nodes.name: Conclude c=b
nodes.statement:
Combining \eqref{eqn: c1} and \eqref{eqn: c2} we find
\begin{align*}c(r)=&\int\limits_{-1}^{i}\psi_T(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz+\int\limits_{1}^{i}\psi_T(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz
-2\int\limits_{0}^{i}\psi_I(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz\\
&-2\int\limits_{i}^{i\infty}\psi_S(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz\\
=&b(r).
 \end{align*}
nodes.section: 4 Fourier eigenfunctions with double zeroes at lattice points
nodes.statement_short: Combine to obtain b(r).

nodes.name: Analogous to Proposition 3
nodes.statement: The proof is analogous to the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop: a another integral}.
nodes.section: 4 Fourier eigenfunctions with double zeroes at lattice points
nodes.statement_short: Follow the proof of Proposition 3.

nodes.name: Apply Proposition 6
nodes.statement:
First, suppose that $r>\sqrt{2}$. Then by Proposition~\ref{prop: b(r) double zeroes}
$$b(r)=4i\,\sin(\pi r^2/2)^2\,\int\limits_{0}^{\infty}\psi_I(it)\,e^{-\pi r^2 t}\,dt. $$
nodes.section: 4 Fourier eigenfunctions with double zeroes at lattice points
nodes.statement_short: For r>sqrt2 use the double-zero representation of b.

nodes.name: Asymptotics of psi_I(it)
nodes.section: 4 Fourier eigenfunctions with double zeroes at lattice points
nodes.statement_short: psi_I(it)=e^{2 pi t}+144+O(e^{-pi t}).

nodes.name: Integrate growing terms
nodes.section: 4 Fourier eigenfunctions with double zeroes at lattice points
nodes.statement_short: Laplace-integrate the growing terms; identity holds for r>sqrt2.

nodes.name: Analyticity of b
nodes.statement: On the other hand, from the definition \eqref{eqn: b(r) definition} we see that $b(r)$ is analytic in some neighborhood of $[0,\infty)$.
nodes.section: 4 Fourier eigenfunctions with double zeroes at lattice points
nodes.statement_short: b is analytic near [0,infinity).

nodes.name: Analytic continuation
nodes.statement: The asymptotic expansion \eqref{eqn: psi asymptotic} implies that the right hand side of \eqref{eqn: b another integral} is also analytic in some neighborhood of $[0,\infty)$. Hence, the identity \eqref{eqn: b another integral} holds on the whole interval $[0,\infty)$. This finishes the proof of the proposition.
nodes.section: 4 Fourier eigenfunctions with double zeroes at lattice points
nodes.statement_short: Extend the identity to all r>=0.

nodes.name: Proof of (g1)
nodes.section: 5 Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: Prove g<=0 beyond sqrt2 by showing A(t)<0.

nodes.name: Laplace representation of g
nodes.section: 5 Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: Write g(r) as sin^2 times a Laplace transform of A(t).

nodes.name: Goal A<0
nodes.section: 5 Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to negativity of A on (0,infinity).

nodes.name: Two presentations of A
nodes.section: 5 Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: Express A near 0 and near infinity via transformation laws.

nodes.name: Asymptotic expansions of A
nodes.section: 5 Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: Define truncated expansions A_0^{(n)}, A_infty^{(n)}.

nodes.name: Compute A_infty^(6)
nodes.statement:
For example, from \eqref{eqn: phi fourier4}--\eqref{eqn: phi fourier0} and \eqref{eqn: psi fourier I} we compute

\begin{align*}A_\infty^{(6)}(t)=&\scriptstyle-\tfrac{72}{\pi ^2}\, e^{2 \pi  t}-\tfrac{23328}{\pi ^2}+\tfrac{184320}{\pi ^2}\, e^{-\pi  t}-\tfrac{5194368}{\pi ^2}\, e^{-2 \pi  t}+\tfrac{22560768}{\pi ^2}\, e^{-3 \pi  t}-\tfrac{250583040}{\pi
   ^2}\, e^{-4 \pi  t}+\tfrac{869916672 }{\pi ^2}\,e^{-5 \pi  t}\\&\scriptstyle+t(\tfrac{8640}{\pi }+\tfrac{2436480}{\pi }\, e^{-2 \pi  t}+\tfrac{113011200 }{\pi }\,e^{-4 \pi  t})-t^2(518400\,e^{-2 \pi  t}+31104000\,e^{-4 \pi  t}).
\end{align*}
nodes.section: 5 Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: Explicit A_infty^{(6)}.

nodes.name: Compute A_0^(6)
nodes.statement:
From \eqref{eqn: phi fourier4}--\eqref{eqn: phi fourier0} and \eqref{eqn: psi fourier S} we compute

$$A_0^{(6)}(t)=t^2(-\tfrac{368640}{\pi ^2}\, e^{-\pi/t}-518400\, e^{-2\pi/t}-\tfrac{45121536}{\pi ^2}\, e^{-3\pi/t}-31104000\,e^{-4\pi/t}-\tfrac{1739833344}{\pi ^2}\, e^{-5\pi/t}).$$
nodes.section: 5 Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: Explicit A_0^{(6)}.

nodes.name: Coefficient bound for psi_I
nodes.statement:
Moreover, from the convergent asymptotic expansion for the Fourier coefficients of a weakly holomorphic modular form \cite[Proposition 1.12]{Bruinier} we find that the $n$-th Fourier coefficient $c_{\psi_I}(n)$ of $\psi_I$ satisfies
\begin{equation} |c_{\psi_I}(n)|\leq e^{4\pi\sqrt{n}}\qquad n\in\tfrac 12 \mathbb{Z}_{>0}.\end{equation}
nodes.section: 5 Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: Bruinier's expansion bounds |c_{psi_I}(n)|.

nodes.name: Coefficient bounds for other forms
nodes.statement:
Similar inequalities hold for the Fourier coefficients of $\psi_S$, $\phi_0$, $\phi_{-2}$, and $\phi_{-4}$:
\begin{align} &|c_{\psi_S}(n)|\leq 2e^{4\pi\sqrt{n}}\qquad n\in\tfrac 12 \mathbb{Z}_{>0} ,\\
&|c_{\phi_0}(n)|\leq 2e^{4\pi\sqrt{n}}\qquad n\in \mathbb{Z}_{>0} ,\\
&|c_{\phi_{-2}}(n)|\leq e^{4\pi\sqrt{n}}\qquad n\in  \mathbb{Z}_{>0},\\
&|c_{\phi_{-4}}(n)|\leq e^{4\pi\sqrt{n}}\qquad n\in \mathbb{Z}_{>0}. \end{align}
nodes.section: 5 Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: Analogous bounds for psi_S, phi_0, phi_{-2}, phi_{-4}.

nodes.name: Error terms
nodes.section: 5 Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: Bound the truncation errors of A.

nodes.name: Define R
nodes.section: 5 Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: Name the error bounds R_0^{(m)}, R_infty^{(m)}.

nodes.name: Interval arithmetic check for A
nodes.statement:
Using interval arithmetic we check that
\begin{align*}
&\left|R_0^{(6)}(t)\right|\leq\left|A_0^{(6)}(t)\right|\quad\mbox{ for }\;t\in(0,1],\\
&\left|R_\infty^{(6)}(t)\right|\leq\left|A_\infty^{(6)}(t)\right|\quad\mbox{ for }\;t\in[1,\infty),\\
&A_0^{(6)}(t)<0\quad\mbox{ for }\;t\in(0,1],\\
&A_\infty^{(6)}(t)<0\quad\mbox{ for }\;t\in[1,\infty).
\end{align*}
nodes.section: 5 Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: Computer-verified inequalities on (0,1] and [1,infinity).

nodes.name: Conclude (g1)
nodes.statement: Thus, we see that $A(t)<0$ for $t\in (0,\infty)$. Then identity \eqref{eqn: g A} implies \eqref{eqn: g1}.
nodes.section: 5 Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: A<0, hence g<=0 for r>sqrt2.

nodes.name: Proof of (g2)
nodes.section: 5 Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: Prove ghat>=0 by showing B(t)>0.

nodes.name: Laplace representation of ghat
nodes.section: 5 Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: Write ghat(r) as sin^2 times a Laplace transform of B(t).

nodes.name: Two presentations of B
nodes.section: 5 Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: Express B near 0 and near infinity.

nodes.name: Goal B>0
nodes.section: 5 Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to positivity of B.

nodes.name: Asymptotic expansions of B
nodes.section: 5 Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: Define truncated expansions of B.

nodes.name: Compute B expansions
nodes.statement:
We find
\begin{align*}B_\infty^{(6)}(t)=&-\tfrac{12960}{\pi ^2}-\tfrac{184320}{\pi ^2}\,\scriptstyle e^{-\pi  t}\displaystyle-\tfrac{116640}{\pi ^2} \,\scriptstyle e^{-2\pi  t}\displaystyle-\tfrac{22560768}{\pi ^2}\,\scriptstyle e^{-3\pi  t}\displaystyle+\tfrac{56540160}{\pi ^2}\,\scriptstyle e^{-4\pi  t}\displaystyle-\tfrac{869916672 }{\pi ^2} \,\scriptstyle e^{-5\pi  t}\displaystyle\\&+t(\tfrac{8640 }{\pi }+\tfrac{2436480}{\pi }\,\scriptstyle e^{-2\pi  t}\displaystyle+\tfrac{113011200 }{\pi }\,\scriptstyle e^{-4\pi  t}\textstyle)-t^2(\scriptstyle518400\,\scriptstyle e^{-2\pi  t}\displaystyle+\scriptstyle31104000\,\scriptstyle e^{-4\pi  t}\displaystyle)
\end{align*}
and
$$B_0^{(6)}(t)= t^2(\tfrac{368640}{\pi ^2}\, e^{-\pi/t}-518400\, e^{-2 \pi /t}+\tfrac{45121536 }{\pi ^2}\,e^{-3 \pi/t}-31104000\, e^{-4 \pi/t}+\tfrac{1739833344 }{\pi ^2}\,e^{-5 \pi/t}) .$$
nodes.section: 5 Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: Explicit B_infty^{(6)} and B_0^{(6)}.

nodes.name: Error bounds for B
nodes.statement:
The estimates \eqref{eqn: Fourier estimate 1}--\eqref{eqn: Fourier estimate 5} imply that $$\left|B(t)-B_0^{(6)}(t)\right|\leq R_0^{(6)}(t)\quad\mbox{for}\;t\in(0,1]$$
and
$$\left|B(t)-B_\infty^{(6)}(t)\right|\leq R_\infty^{(6)}(t)\quad\mbox{for}\;t\in[1,\infty).$$
nodes.section: 5 Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: Same error bounds R apply to B.

nodes.name: Interval arithmetic check for B
nodes.statement:
Using interval arithmetic we verify that
\begin{align*}
&\left|R_0^{(6)}(t)\right|\leq\left|B_0^{(6)}(t)\right|\quad\mbox{ for }\;t\in(0,1],\\
&\left|R_\infty^{(6)}(t)\right|\leq\left|B_\infty^{(6)}(t)\right|\quad\mbox{ for }\;t\in[1,\infty),\\
&B_0^{(6)}(t)>0\quad\mbox{ for }\;t\in(0,1],\\
&B_\infty^{(6)}(t)>0\quad\mbox{ for }\;t\in[1,\infty).
\end{align*}
nodes.section: 5 Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: Computer-verified inequalities for B.

nodes.name: Conclude (g2)
nodes.statement: Now identity \eqref{eqn: g B} implies \eqref{eqn: g2}.
nodes.section: 5 Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: B>0, hence ghat>=0.

nodes.name: Proof of (g3)
nodes.statement:
Finally, the property \eqref{eqn: g3} readily follows from Proposition~\ref{prop: a values} and Proposition~\ref{prop: b values}.
This finishes the proof of Theorems~\ref{thm: g1} and~\ref{thm: g}.

nodes.statement_short: Normalisation from the special values of a and b.
